WA looks to turn resources into industrial advantage

by Adam Daunt
September 16, 2026
in News
Reading Time: 2 mins read
A A

WA MLA David Scaife delivered the opening address at WA Mining 2026. Image: Prime Creative Media

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 2:02
Instaread

Western Australia will look to leverage decades of mining investment and expertise to build a broader industrial advantage as the state plans its next phase of resources growth.

At the opening of the WA Mining Conference and Exhibition 2026,  WA member of the legislative assembly David Scaife said WA’s mineral and petroleum industries generated about $225 billion in sales last year, directly supported around 136,000 full-time equivalent jobs, and returned $10.6 billion in royalties and related revenue to the state.

Mining and petroleum investment reached $34 billion, representing 62 per cent of Australian investment across the two sectors.

Scaife said the figures demonstrated not only the continuing importance of resources to WA, but the industrial capability developed around the sector.

“We’re fortunate here in Western Australia not to have to talk about reindustrialisation because we have kept and expanded our industrial capability, thanks to the investment and the work of the resources industry,” he said.

The next challenge was to leverage that capability in areas including downstream processing and defence.

Scaife said WA’s experienced workforce, engineering and mining services businesses, ports, railways, energy networks and industrial land were foundations for further development.

However, he said a shortage of available industrial land was among the constraints the government was working to address.

“We don’t want to move away from mining,” Scaife said.

“It is our core capability and strength here in Western Australia, but a lot of our best opportunities grow out of the mining industry.”

Approvals reform will also form part of that agenda, as Scaife said companies need decisions within reasonable, predictable timeframes.

He said the government would continue looking for opportunities to process approvals in parallel and reduce duplication between state and federal processes while maintaining environmental and heritage standards.

Scaife said WA’s geology provided a head start, but future investment would depend on more than its resources endowment.

“We are in a global race for capital,” he said.

“We know that here in the WA government and we have to win that race.”
